bibl.title: A conceptual framework for implementation fidelity

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A CONCEPT RE-PARTITIONED RATHER THAN REDEFINED - implementation fidelity keeps all five of the elements the literature gives it, and this paper changes what they are TO EACH OTHER: adherence becomes the measurement, two become moderators, one is expelled and renamed, and two new moderators are added
span.quote: The concept of implementation fidelity is currently described and defined in the literature in terms of five elements that need to be measured [ 1 , 2 , 4 ]. These are: adherence to an intervention; exposure or dose; quality of delivery; participant responsiveness; and programme differentiation. There are certain overlaps here with the concept of process evaluation [ 15 ].

span.label: what implementation fidelity IS, given that the same five elements are read by one camp as five alternative measures and by another as five components all of which must be measured
span.quote: Despite agreeing that implementation fidelity involves measurement of these five elements, the review literature offers two distinct views on how this should be done. On the one hand, it is argued that each of these five elements represents an alternative way to measure fidelity, i.e ., implementation fidelity can be measured using either adherence or dosage or quality of delivery etc [ 4 , 5 ]. On the other hand, it is argued that all five elements need to be measured to capture a "comprehensive" or "more complete picture" of the process, i.e ., evaluation requires the measurement of adherence, dosage, and quality of delivery, etc [ 1 , 2 ]. However, relationships between the various elements are far more complex than such conceptualisations allow.

span.label: a framework in which adherence (content, coverage, frequency, duration) is the measurement of fidelity, moderated by intervention complexity, facilitation strategies, quality of delivery and participant responsiveness - with programme differentiation removed from the concept altogether
span.quote: The measurement of implementation fidelity is the measurement of adherence, i.e ., how far those responsible for delivering an intervention actually adhere to the intervention as it is outlined by its designers. Adherence includes the subcategories of content, frequency, duration and coverage ( i.e ., dose). The degree to which the intended content or frequency of an intervention is implemented is the degree of implementation fidelity achieved for that intervention. The level achieved may be influenced or affected, ( i.e ., moderated) by certain other variables: intervention complexity, facilitation strategies, quality of delivery, and participant responsiveness.

span.label: method
span.quote: This paper therefore advances a new, third conceptual framework for implementation fidelity, which not only proposes the measurement of all of these elements, but unlike all previous attempts to make sense of this concept also clarifies and explains the function of each and their relationship to one another. Two additional elements are also introduced into this new framework: intervention complexity and facilitation strategies.

span.label: the gap between an intervention as designed and as delivered, which decides whether a null result means the programme failed or the delivery did
span.quote: It is only by making an appropriate evaluation of the fidelity with which an intervention has been implemented that a viable assessment can be made of its contribution to outcomes, i.e ., its effect on performance. Unless such an evaluation is made, it cannot be determined whether a lack of impact is due to poor implementation or inadequacies inherent in the programme itself, a so-called Type III error [ 11 ]; this is also addressed by the thesis of comprehensiveness [ 12 ].

span.label: a critical review of the implementation-fidelity literature from 2002 to 2007 across five databases, with the earlier reviews taken as given, and a framework built from the limitations found
span.term: a critical review of the implementation-fidelity literature from 2002 to 2007 across five databases, with the earlier reviews taken as given, and a framework built from the limitations found
span.quote: The concept of implementation fidelity is currently described and defined in the literature in terms of five elements that need to be measured [ 1 , 2 , 4 ]. These are: adherence to an intervention; exposure or dose; quality of delivery; participant responsiveness; and programme differentiation. There are certain overlaps here with the concept of process evaluation [ 15 ].

span.label: **THE SAME FIVE PARTS, RE-RANKED**: the literature has `adherence to an intervention; exposure or dose; quality of delivery; participant responsiveness; and programme differentiation`. This paper keeps every one and changes what they are to each other - `THE MEASUREMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION FIDELITY IS THE MEASUREMENT OF ADHERENCE ... The level achieved MAY BE INFLUENCED OR AFFECTED, ( i.e ., MODERATED) BY certain other variables: INTERVENTION COMPLEXITY, FACILITATION STRATEGIES, QUALITY OF DELIVERY, AND PARTICIPANT RESPONSIVENESS.` **A definition changed by rearranging its parts rather than by adding or removing them**
span.quote: The measurement of implementation fidelity is the measurement of adherence, i.e ., how far those responsible for delivering an intervention actually adhere to the intervention as it is outlined by its designers. Adherence includes the subcategories of content, frequency, duration and coverage ( i.e ., dose). The degree to which the intended content or frequency of an intervention is implemented is the degree of implementation fidelity achieved for that intervention. The level achieved may be influenced or affected, ( i.e ., moderated) by certain other variables: intervention complexity, facilitation strategies, quality of delivery, and participant responsiveness.

span.label: **AND ONE PART IS EXPELLED FROM THE CONCEPT AND RENAMED**: `DESPITE BEING VIEWED AS AN ELEMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION FIDELITY BY THE LITERATURE, PROGRAMME DIFFERENTIATION ACTUALLY MEASURES SOMETHING DISTINCT FROM FIDELITY. It is concerned with determining those elements that are essential for its success ... THIS ELEMENT WOULD THEREFORE BE MORE USEFULLY DESCRIBED AS THE `IDENTIFICATION OF AN INTERVENTION'S ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS`.` **A component removed from a concept because it measures a different thing, and given a name that says what it does measure**
span.quote: Despite being viewed as an element of implementation fidelity by the literature, programme differentiation actually measures something distinct from fidelity. It is concerned with determining those elements that are essential for its success. This exercise is an important part of any evaluation of new interventions. It enables discovery of those elements that make a difference to outcomes and whether some elements are redundant. Such so-called "essential" elements may be discovered either by canvassing the designers of the intervention or, preferably, by "component analysis", assessing the effect of the intervention on outcomes and determining which components have the most impact [ 17 ]. This element would therefore be more usefully described as the "Identification of an intervention's essential components".

span.label: **AND THE FIELD COULD NOT AGREE WHETHER ITS DEFINITION WAS AN `AND` OR AN `OR`**: `the review literature offers TWO DISTINCT VIEWS ... On the one hand, it is argued that EACH OF THESE FIVE ELEMENTS REPRESENTS AN ALTERNATIVE WAY TO MEASURE FIDELITY, i.e., implementation fidelity can be measured using EITHER ADHERENCE OR DOSAGE OR QUALITY OF DELIVERY etc. On the other hand, it is argued that ALL FIVE ELEMENTS NEED TO BE MEASURED to capture a `comprehensive` ... picture.` **One five-part definition, read as a disjunction by one camp and a conjunction by the other** - the connective was never written down, and two literatures grew on either side of it
span.quote: Despite agreeing that implementation fidelity involves measurement of these five elements, the review literature offers two distinct views on how this should be done. On the one hand, it is argued that each of these five elements represents an alternative way to measure fidelity, i.e ., implementation fidelity can be measured using either adherence or dosage or quality of delivery etc [ 4 , 5 ]. On the other hand, it is argued that all five elements need to be measured to capture a "comprehensive" or "more complete picture" of the process, i.e ., evaluation requires the measurement of adherence, dosage, and quality of delivery, etc [ 1 , 2 ]. However, relationships between the various elements are far more complex than such conceptualisations allow.

span.label: AND THE CANONICAL DEFINITION IS QUOTED WITH HOLES IN IT: `Implementation fidelity is `THE DEGREE TO WHICH . . . PROGRAMS ARE IMPLEMENTED . . . AS INTENDED BY THE PROGRAM DEVELOPERS`. This idea is SOMETIMES ALSO TERMED `INTEGRITY`.` **Two elisions inside a one-line definition**, in the opening sentence of the paper - and a synonym recorded in the next breath
span.quote: Implementation fidelity is "the degree to which . . . programs are implemented . . . as intended by the program developers" [ 1 ]. This idea is sometimes also termed "integrity" [ 1 , 2 ].

span.label: AND THE REASON ANY OF IT MATTERS IS A NAMED ERROR: `Unless such an evaluation is made, IT CANNOT BE DETERMINED WHETHER A LACK OF IMPACT IS DUE TO POOR IMPLEMENTATION OR INADEQUACIES INHERENT IN THE PROGRAMME ITSELF, A SO-CALLED TYPE III ERROR.` **Without a fidelity measurement, a null result cannot be attributed** - the intervention and its delivery are confounded by construction
span.quote: It is only by making an appropriate evaluation of the fidelity with which an intervention has been implemented that a viable assessment can be made of its contribution to outcomes, i.e ., its effect on performance. Unless such an evaluation is made, it cannot be determined whether a lack of impact is due to poor implementation or inadequacies inherent in the programme itself, a so-called Type III error [ 11 ]; this is also addressed by the thesis of comprehensiveness [ 12 ].

span.label: AND THE SAME GAP BREAKS SYNTHESIS: `the common LACK OF DATA ON IMPLEMENTATION FIDELITY provided by primary research studies, KNOWN AS `THINNESS`, prevents those working on systematic reviews and meta-analyses FROM GAUGING POSSIBLE HETEROGENEITY BETWEEN STUDIES, with the result that DATA MAY BE POOLED OR AGGREGATED INAPPROPRIATELY.` A named defect - `thinness` - for a missing measurement, and a direct route from it to a wrong pooled estimate
span.quote: Similar issues affect secondary research: the common lack of data on implementation fidelity provided by primary research studies, known as "thinness", prevents those working on systematic reviews and meta-analyses from gauging possible heterogeneity between studies, with the result that data may be pooled or aggregated inappropriately [ 13 , 14 ]. Consequently, the internal validity of a review may be adversely affected, and, thus, the credibility and utility of that research may be thrown into question.

span.label: AND THE MODERATORS ARE PROPOSED WITH THEIR EVIDENCE STATED AS ABSENT: `Although some studies have claimed that the provision of certain facilitation strategies has positively affected implementation ..., THESE CLAIMS ARE NOT THE RESULT OF EMPIRICAL RESEARCH. However, NO STUDY HAS YET MEASURED THE MODERATING EFFECT of these strategies on the degree of implementation fidelity.` **A framework that names the cell of the table it cannot fill**, and says so about its own new element
span.quote: Although some studies have claimed that the provision of certain facilitation strategies has positively affected implementation of an intervention, these claims are not the result of empirical research [ 13 ]. However, no study has yet measured the moderating effect of these strategies on the degree of implementation fidelity.

span.label: AND THE MODERATORS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT: `One reason is THE MODERATING ROLE OF INTERVENTION COMPLEXITY: a simple intervention may not require much training or guidance to achieve high quality of delivery or participant responsiveness ... there may be INTERACTION EFFECTS BETWEEN MODERATORS, i.e ., WHEN THE EFFECT OF ONE FACTOR IS DEPENDENT ON THE LEVEL OF ANOTHER.` And on amount versus adequacy: `MORE FACILITATION STRATEGIES DO NOT NECESSARILY MEAN BETTER IMPLEMENTATION`
span.quote: One reason is the moderating role of intervention complexity: A simple intervention may not require much training or guidance to achieve high quality of delivery or participant responsiveness. A small amount of training may suffice. In other words, there may be interaction effects between moderators, i.e ., when the effect of one factor is dependent on the level of another.

span.label: AND FIDELITY IS SET AGAINST ADAPTATION, WITH AN INTERMEDIATE POSITION: `the PRO-ADAPTATION PERSPECTIVE implies that SUCCESSFUL INTERVENTIONS ARE THOSE THAT ADAPT TO LOCAL NEEDS. However, some argue that the case for local adaptation MAY WELL HAVE BEEN EXAGGERATED ... THE INTERMEDIATE POSITION IS THEREFORE THAT PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION CAN BE FLEXIBLE AS LONG AS THERE IS FIDELITY TO THE SO-CALLED `ESSENTIAL` ELEMENTS.` **The essential components are what makes flexibility measurable** - and the paper immediately concedes `the question remains about HOW TO IDENTIFY WHAT IS ESSENTIAL`
span.quote: Identifying these essential components also provides scope for identifying adaptability to local conditions. An intervention cannot always be implemented fully in the real world. Local conditions may require it to be flexible and adaptable. Some specifications of interventions allow for local adaptation. Even if they do not explicitly do this, local adaptations may be made to improve the fit of the intervention within the local context. Indeed, the pro-adaptation perspective implies that successful interventions are those that adapt to local needs [ 22 ]. However, some argue that the case for local adaptation may well have been exaggerated, at least for interventions where the evidence does not necessarily support it [ 3 ]. The intermediate position is therefore that programme implementation can be flexible as long as there is fidelity to the so-called "essential" elements of an intervention.

span.label: AND WHAT THE FIELD ACTUALLY MEASURES IS ONE ELEMENT: `most implementation fidelity research FOCUSES SOLELY ON A FIDELITY SCORE DETERMINED ALMOST EXCLUSIVELY BY ADHERENCE. Moreover, this research RARELY REPORTS HIGH IMPLEMENTATION FIDELITY. It actually often FALLS SHORT OF THE IDEAL AND IS SOMETIMES EVEN VERY POOR, yet it is ONLY BY MEASURING THE MODERATORS ... that potential explanations for low or inadequate implementation MAY BE APPREHENDED.` **The one element everyone measures is the one the framework says is an outcome of the other four**
span.quote: With the exception of a few studies that do measure quality of delivery or participant responsiveness [ 8 , 20 , 38 ], most implementation fidelity research focuses solely on a fidelity score determined almost exclusively by adherence [ 3 , 6 - 8 , 21 , 22 , 27 - 29 , 38 , 39 ]. Moreover, this research rarely reports high implementation fidelity [ 8 , 29 , 40 ]. It actually often falls short of the ideal and is sometimes even very poor, yet it is only by measuring the moderators described above that potential explanations for low or inadequate implementation may be apprehended or understood.

span.label: **THE FRAMEWORK IS UNTESTED AND THE PAPER LEADS WITH IT**: the abstract says `THE RESULTING THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK REQUIRES TESTING BY EMPIRICAL RESEARCH`, and the summary repeats it - `EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IS NEEDED TO TEST THE FRAMEWORK ITSELF AND TO CLARIFY THE MODERATING IMPACT OF THE COMPONENTS INCLUDED HERE.` A conceptual rearrangement of an existing literature, offered as one, and cited 2,618 times
span.quote: This conceptualisation provides researchers with a potential framework for implementation research. Monitoring of implementation fidelity following this framework enables better evaluation of the actual impact of an intervention on outcomes. In turn, the credibility and utility of the resulting research would be enhanced accordingly. It also offers evidence-based practitioners a guide to the processes and factors at play when implementing interventions described in research. However, much more research is needed on this topic. Empirical research is needed to test the framework itself and to clarify the moderating impact of the components included here.

span.label: AND ONE OF THE TWO NEW MODERATORS HAS NO EVIDENCE AT ALL: `NO STUDY HAS YET MEASURED THE MODERATING EFFECT of these strategies on the degree of implementation fidelity`, and the claims that do exist `ARE NOT THE RESULT OF EMPIRICAL RESEARCH`. **The element is added on the strength of a systematic review about a different question** - the diffusion of innovations in organisations
span.quote: Although some studies have claimed that the provision of certain facilitation strategies has positively affected implementation of an intervention, these claims are not the result of empirical research [ 13 ]. However, no study has yet measured the moderating effect of these strategies on the degree of implementation fidelity.

span.label: AND THE PIVOT OF THE FRAMEWORK - `ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS` - HAS NO PROCEDURE: `the question remains about HOW TO IDENTIFY WHAT IS ESSENTIAL. One possible way ... is to conduct a sensitivity analysis, or `component analysis`, USING IMPLEMENTATION FIDELITY DATA AND PERFORMANCE OUTCOMES FROM DIFFERENT STUDIES OF THE SAME INTERVENTION ... HOWEVER, IF ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS OF AN INTERVENTION ARE NOT KNOWN, THEN FIDELITY TO THE WHOLE INTERVENTION IS NEEDED.` **The method for finding the essential components requires the fidelity data that the framework exists to produce**
span.quote: However, adherence may not require every single component of an intervention to be implemented. An intervention may also be implemented successfully, and meaningfully, if only the "essential" components of the model are implemented. However, the question remains about how to identify what is essential. One possible way to do this is to conduct a sensitivity analysis, or "component analysis", using implementation fidelity data and performance outcomes from different studies of the same intervention to determine which, if any, components or combination of components are essential, i.e ., are prerequisite if the intervention is to have its desired effect. However, if essential components of an intervention are not known, then fidelity to the whole intervention is needed.

span.label: AND `QUALITY OF DELIVERY` IS LEFT IN TWO PLACES AT ONCE: `IF SUCH A CLEAR BENCHMARK EXISTS then quality of delivery MAY BE TREATED, ALONG WITH ADHERENCE AND DOSAGE, AS ONE OF THREE DISCRETE ASPECTS required to assess the fidelity of an intervention. HOWEVER, IT MAY POTENTIALLY ALSO BE VIEWED AS A MODERATOR ... THIS IS A ROLE THAT IS SIMPLY NOT EXPLORED IN THE LITERATURE TO DATE.` The framework files it as a moderator; the paragraph that argues for it says it depends on whether a benchmark exists. **A component whose place in the concept is conditional on the availability of a measurement**
span.quote: If such a clear benchmark exists then quality of delivery may be treated, along with adherence and dosage, as one of three discrete aspects required to assess the fidelity of an intervention. However, it may potentially also be viewed as a moderator of the relationship between an intervention and the fidelity with which it is implemented. This is a role that is simply not explored in the literature to date. For example, an intervention could be delivered but delivered badly; in turn, the degree of fidelity achieved by the implemented intervention could be adversely affected.

span.label: keeping programme differentiation OUT of the fidelity measurement and giving it its own name
span.note: eliminates: a fidelity score contaminated by a judgement about which components matter · outcome: held
span.quote: Despite being viewed as an element of implementation fidelity by the literature, programme differentiation actually measures something distinct from fidelity. It is concerned with determining those elements that are essential for its success. This exercise is an important part of any evaluation of new interventions. It enables discovery of those elements that make a difference to outcomes and whether some elements are redundant. Such so-called "essential" elements may be discovered either by canvassing the designers of the intervention or, preferably, by "component analysis", assessing the effect of the intervention on outcomes and determining which components have the most impact [ 17 ]. This element would therefore be more usefully described as the "Identification of an intervention's essential components".

span.label: requiring fidelity to the whole intervention wherever the essential components are unknown
span.note: eliminates: an implementer choosing which parts to drop and still claiming high fidelity · outcome: held

However, if essential components of an intervention are not known, then fidelity to the whole intervention is needed.

Dosage or exposure refers to the amount of an intervention received by participants; in other words, whether the frequency and duration of the intervention is as full as prescribed by its designers [ 1 , 4 ].

span.term: the fidelity with which an intervention is implemented
span.quote: It has been demonstrated that the fidelity with which an intervention is implemented affects how well it succeeds [ 1 - 5 ].

span.label: how well it succeeds
span.quote: It has been demonstrated that the fidelity with which an intervention is implemented affects how well it succeeds [ 1 - 5 ].

span.label: Specificity
span.quote: Detailed or specific interventions have been found to be more likely to be implemented with high fidelity than ones that are vague. For example, a study of guidelines intended for General Practitioners (GPs) found that detailed and clear recommendations were almost twice as likely to be followed as vague and non-specific recommendations [ 23 ]. The specificity of these guidelines was assessed by a group of researchers and their uptake was evaluated by the GPs' self-report. In the same way, well-planned interventions, where all the key components are identified in advance, have been found to produce higher levels of adherence than less well-structured interventions [ 1 , 5 ]. Specificity enhances adherence.
